1. Core Clinical Tension: A 53-year-old West African immigrant presents with a 14-year history of fluctuating digestive complaints (abdominal pain, diarrhea alternating with constipation) and recurrent cutaneous lesions (subcutaneous nodules and transient linear rashes). The central clinical trap is the complete lack of peripheral eosinophilia on routine blood counts, which previously diverted clinicians toward irritable bowel syndrome or non-parasitic dermatologic disorders.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission narrative stops after reviewing the 14-year history of gastrointestinal symptoms, documented subcutaneous nodules and leg eruptions, and routine complete blood count demonstrating the absence of eosinophilia, prior to parasite-specific serologic testing.
3. Differential Distinctions: Functional bowel disorders and idiopathic dermatitides can account for alternating bowel habits and non-specific rashes but fail to explain mobile subcutaneous nodules or transient migratory linear/longitudinal desquamating trunk eruptions; positive parasite-specific IgG establishes the chronic autoinfective helminthiasis.
case_prompt: A 53-year-old male who emigrated from Mali 25 years ago presented with subcutaneous skin nodules in the periumbilical area and left lower quadrant that had been present for 5 years. He also reported a 14-year history of intermittent abdominal pain, nausea, and diarrhea alternating with constipation, as well as an intermittent maculopapular rash on his legs. He noted occasional use of herbal remedies without symptomatic relief. Two months prior to evaluation, he noted a 3 cm x 14 cm longitudinal desquamative maculopapular rash along the midline of his back that cleared spontaneously over 2 weeks. On physical examination, two 0.5 cm mobile subcutaneous nodules were palpated in the left lower quadrant and periumbilical region, and one in the gluteal region, with normal overlying skin. Examination of the legs revealed scattered areas of maculopapular rash. The remainder of the physical examination was normal. Complete blood count showed no eosinophilia.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Irritable Bowel Syndrome / Functional Bowel Disorder
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered because of 14 years of fluctuating abdominal pain, nausea, and alternating diarrhea and constipation without systemic signs on routine CBC; ruled out because functional disorders cannot explain subcutaneous nodules or migratory linear cutaneous lesions.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: intermittent abdominal pain, nausea, and diarrhea, alternating with constipation, which were all present for the past 14 years. During this time, the patient had seen many physicians without a definitive diagnosis and without effective treatment.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to recurrent maculopapular eruptions and lack of peripheral blood eosinophilia; ruled out because the transient longitudinal morphology on the back reflected larval cutaneous migration (larva currens) and symptoms cleared completely following anthelmintic therapy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The complete blood count did not indicate eosinophilia.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The diagnostic turning point was identifying the combination of decades-long geographic residency risk, chronic gastrointestinal disturbance, and transient migratory linear trunk rash, confirmed by positive anti-strongyloidiasis IgG serology despite normal eosinophil counts.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: However, the patient's serology for anti-strongyloidiasis IgG was positive.

editor_comments: Distilled strictly to baseline admission presentation. Atypical absence of peripheral eosinophilia in a 25-year chronic infection; confirmed by serology and complete resolution with ivermectin.
